Female European flying squid attain a maximum mantle length at death of approximately 75.0 centimeters [Li = approximately 75.0 centimeters], whereas males reach a significantly smaller terminal size of 64.0 centimeters [Li = 64.0 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in final body size is common among ommastrephid squids and is generally attributed to differential reproductive energetics, with females investing heavily in somatic growth to support the production of large egg masses. Hatchlings emerge from the egg capsule at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth estimated at 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of related illexine squids. This minuscule neonatal mass reflects the planktonic strategy of the paralarval stage, during which individuals must rapidly begin exogenous feeding on small zooplankton to fuel their exponential growth trajectory. The transition from the yolk-dependent embryo to a free-swimming, exogenously feeding larva represents a critical bottleneck in the species' early life history.

Onset of sexual maturity, as indicated by the initiation of gonad maturation, occurs at a mantle length of 23.6 centimeters [Lp = 23.6 centimeters] in females, while males become reproductively active at a smaller mantle length of 20.0 centimeters [Lp = 20.0 centimeters]. These values represent the size at which the first spermatophores or oocytes become detectable in the reproductive system, marking the physiological transition to the sub-adult phase. The earlier attainment of puberty in males is a pattern observed across many cephalopod species and is thought to be linked to the lower energetic cost of spermatophore production compared to the substantial investment required for egg formation. Field records from the northeastern Atlantic indicate considerable individual variation around these mean values, with female puberty onset ranging broadly from 195 to 330 millimeters in mantle length, reflecting the influence of local environmental conditions such as temperature and food availability on the timing of maturation.

Cumulative reproductive output at death has been estimated at 500,000.0 oocytes  per female under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This high fecundity is characteristic of many ommastrephid squids and represents a life-history strategy that compensates for high early-life mortality in the planktonic environment. The total ovarian complement is deposited in multiple distinct spawning events throughout the terminal portion of the adult female's life, with the eggs being released in gelatinous masses that drift in mid-water currents. Field observations suggest that the realized fecundity in wild populations may be somewhat lower than this laboratory maximum due to constraints imposed by prey availability and the energetic demands of continuous swimming during the spawning migration. Despite these potential reductions, the species remains one of the more fecund cephalopods in its North Atlantic range.

The maximum lifespan for female individuals reaches 365.0 days [am = 365.0 days] at 21 °C [T = 21 °C], a relatively short duration typical of the semelparous life cycle found in most ommastrephid squids. This one-year lifespan at a stable thermal regime aligns with the rapid growth rates and early maturation schedules that define the genus Todarodes. Following the final spawning event, females experience a rapid physiological deterioration, including the loss of skin pigmentation and a reduction in mantle muscle tone, culminating in natural mortality shortly after reproduction. The synchrony of this post-reproductive senescence is thought to be linked to the exhaustion of somatic reserves that are redirected toward egg production during the final weeks of life, a pattern that is also well-documented in other short-lived coleoid cephalopods such as the common octopus and the Pacific flying squid.

The species exhibits a classic r-selected life-history strategy, characterized by a small hatchling mass of just 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams], rapid juvenile growth, early puberty at 23.6 centimeters [Lp = 23.6 centimeters] in females and 20.0 centimeters [Lp = 20.0 centimeters] in males, and a terminal mantle length that differs substantially between the sexes. In comparative terms, the maximum female mantle length of 75.0 centimeters [Li = 75.0 centimeters] is larger than that recorded for the congeneric Todarodes filippovae but smaller than the maximum sizes reported for the jumbo squid Dosidicus gigas from the eastern Pacific. The cumulative lifetime fecundity of half a million oocytes per female (500,000.0 oocytes) , realized within a single year under optimal thermal conditions at 21 °C [T = 21 °C], underscores the extreme reproductive investment that defines the ecology of this commercially important ommastrephid squid across its North Atlantic and Mediterranean range.
